title: Review: Elimination; Ozone depletion and CFCs; Alcohols: oxidation; Mass spectrometry and IR of molecules
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AN01#t2 term and clue written for the game; OR15#t1 term and clue written for the game; OR08#t2 term and clue written for the game; OR15#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AN01#N.6, OR08#N.10b, OR11#N.11, OR15#N.9, AN01#N.4, OR08#N.9, OR11#N.2, OR15#N.11, AN01#N.13, OR11#N.5, OR15#N.2, AN01#N.3. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Greenhouse gas
items.clue: Takes in IR given out by the Earth's surface, then sends it out in all directions.

items.label: Aldehyde
items.clue: First product of oxidising a primary alcohol, e.g. ethanal; distilled off as it forms.

items.label: CFCs
items.clue: Unreactive compounds such as CCl₂F₂, once used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants.

items.label: Ketone
items.clue: Product of oxidising a secondary alcohol, e.g. propanone; it cannot be oxidised further.

questions.stem: A compound gives a molecular ion at m/z = 58.0417 in a high-resolution mass spectrum. Use ¹H 1.0078, ¹²C 12.0000, ¹⁴N 14.0031, ¹⁶O 15.9949. What is its molecular formula?

options.text: C₄H₁₀
C₂H₂O₂
C₃H₆O
C₂H₆N₂

questions.stem: Old fridges leaked a CFC, CCl₃F. Years later it reaches the ozone layer. What happens, and why is the effect so large?

options.text: Each CFC molecule removes one ozone molecule, so the ozone lost equals the CFC leaked.
Chlorine atoms destroy ozone, so less harmful UV radiation reaches the Earth's surface.
UV frees chlorine atoms; each destroys many ozone molecules, letting more UV through.
The CFC absorbs UV high up, so less UV reaches the ground and the ozone is not needed.

questions.explanation: Each chlorine atom is set free again after destroying an ozone molecule: it is a catalyst. The thinner layer lets more harmful UV through.

questions.stem: Chlorocyclohexane is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide in one tube, and heated under reflux with sodium hydroxide in ethanol in another. The main product in the second tube is cyclohexene. Which statement explains the second result?

options.text: In ethanol, OH⁻ bonds to the δ+ carbon of the C–Cl bond, and Cl⁻ leaves.
In ethanol, the solvent removes HCl from chlorocyclohexane, and OH⁻ just neutralises the HCl.
In ethanol, OH⁻ mainly acts as a base, removing H⁺ from a carbon next to the C–Cl carbon.
In ethanol, the ring opens as OH⁻ breaks a C–C bond, and a gaseous product is released.

questions.stem: Three colourless liquids, X, Y and Z, are butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol, in some order. Each is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). X and Y turn the mixture green; Z leaves it orange. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: Z is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, the tertiary alcohol.
Z is butan-1-ol, as primary alcohols are oxidised only under reflux.
X and Y are both primary, as only primary alcohols turn the dichromate green.
The test shows that X is butan-1-ol and Y is butan-2-ol.

questions.explanation: Its C–OH carbon carries no H, so it is not oxidised and the dichromate stays orange.

questions.stem: Methyl butanoate, CH₃CH₂CH₂COOCH₃ (Mr = 102), gives a peak at m/z 71. Which neutral fragment was lost to form this ion?

options.text: CH₃, mass 15
OCH₃, mass 31
A fragment of mass 71
COOH, mass 45

questions.explanation: 102 − 71 = 31: OCH₃. Losing the methoxy group leaves CH₃CH₂CH₂CO⁺ (m/z 71), a sign of a methyl ester.

questions.stem: HFC-134a, CH₂FCF₃, replaced CFCs in fridges. Why doesn't it damage the ozone layer?

options.text: It has no chlorine, so it releases no chlorine atoms high in the atmosphere.
It contains fluorine, and fluorine atoms remove chlorine atoms from the air.
It is more reactive than CFCs, so it reacts with ozone to form harmless products.
Its C–F bonds break easily in UV, but fluorine atoms don't react with ozone.

questions.explanation: Its bonds are C–H, C–F and C–C. None is C–Cl, so no Cl atoms form to start the ozone-destroying cycle.

questions.stem: 2-bromopropane is heated under reflux with potassium hydroxide dissolved in ethanol, and propene forms. What is the role of the hydroxide ion?

options.text: It is a nucleophile: it donates a lone pair to the carbon bonded to Br.
It is an electrophile: it accepts a pair of electrons from the C–Br bond.
It is a base: it accepts H⁺ from a carbon next to the C–Br carbon.
It is a catalyst: it is given back at the end, so it is written over the arrow.

questions.explanation: OH⁻ takes an H⁺ from the neighbouring carbon and becomes H₂O. Br⁻ leaves, and a C=C forms between the two carbons.

questions.stem: A few drops of cyclohexanol, a six-carbon ring with an –OH on one ring carbon, are warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). What do you see, and why?

options.text: It stays orange, as an –OH on a ring carbon makes the alcohol tertiary.
Orange to green: it is oxidised to cyclohexanone as Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced to Cr³⁺.
Orange to green: it is oxidised to a carboxylic acid with six carbons, as Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced.
Orange to green: it is reduced to cyclohexane, while the dichromate(VI) ions are oxidised.

questions.explanation: Secondary alcohol → ketone. The alcohol loses the H from O–H and the H from the C–OH carbon. Dichromate(VI), orange, is reduced to green Cr³⁺.

questions.stem: Compound Q, C₃H₆O, absorbs strongly at 1725 cm⁻¹ and does not absorb between 3200 and 3600 cm⁻¹. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: Q contains C=O and no O–H, so it is an aldehyde or a ketone.
Q contains a C=C bond, so it is prop-2-en-1-ol, CH₂=CHCH₂OH.
Q is an alcohol, since its single O atom must be in an O–H group.
Q must be propanone, since only ketones absorb near 1725 cm⁻¹.

questions.explanation: 1725 cm⁻¹ is a C=O band. No broad band at 3200–3600 rules out an alcohol O–H. With one O atom, Q is propanal or propanone.

questions.stem: A chemist wants as much propene, and as little propan-2-ol, as possible from 2-bromopropane. Which conditions should be used?

options.text: Aqueous potassium hydroxide, warmed gently
Aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol, warmed
Potassium hydroxide with ultraviolet light, at room temperature
Potassium hydroxide dissolved in ethanol, heated under reflux

questions.explanation: Ethanol as the solvent and a high temperature favour OH⁻ acting as a base. Some propan-2-ol still forms, as the two reactions compete.

questions.stem: Which of these is a secondary alcohol?

options.text: Butan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH
Butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃
2-methylpropan-1-ol, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH
2-methylbutan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃

questions.explanation: The C–OH carbon is bonded to two other carbons (CH₃ and CH₂CH₃), so the alcohol is secondary.

questions.stem: Which statement about the molecular ion peak in the mass spectrum of an organic compound is correct?

options.text: It is the tallest peak, as most molecules reach the detector unbroken.
It is due to an ion formed when a molecule gains an electron.
Any peak at lower m/z than it shows an impurity in the sample.
Its m/z value gives the relative molecular mass of the compound.

questions.explanation: M⁺ is the whole molecule minus one electron. With a charge of 1+, its m/z equals Mr.
